## TL;DR

Check gates now cover handoff validation, managed remote-plus-local self-checks, direct CLI checks in a task worktree, and close-out validation. RepoOS queues bookkeeping commits and replays them in order after the last gate holder exits. A failed replay now leaves a durable pending fence, and direct self-checks fail when source commits land during execution. Drift checks report source commit subjects and paths while allowing bookkeeping-only movement. Review 9's accepted limitation remains: direct filesystem writes by an already-running engineer cannot be fenced; committed source drift is detected after the fact.

## Work and rationale

The self-check lock starts before remote validation. In managed runs, the remote helper may take a nested holder, while the outer holder remains through the local plan so there is no remote-to-local gap. A normal `repoos check` in a task worktree discovers the task ID from its branch and task file and acquires the same lock. The WIP checkpoint is written before locking so the check does not block its own checkpoint. The holder is released in the local plan's `finally`; errors and local-slot failures release it too. Handoff and close-out already hold their locks for their full validation windows.

Review 9 found that release and stale recovery ignored a failed queue flush and cleared the lock. The holder release closure, process release, and stale-lock reconciliation now keep the lock as an empty `flushPending` fence when replay fails. Commit routing treats that record as active: new bookkeeping joins the queue, source commits remain refused, and new gates cannot acquire over the pending replay. Recovery retries the queue and clears the fence only after replay succeeds. If an older queue survives without a lock file, recovery reconstructs a pending fence from its queued commit worktree before attempting the replay.

Queue entries preserve explicit write/delete snapshots at enqueue time. A pending journal records the pre-commit HEAD, commit message, prior file snapshots, and intended snapshots before files are changed. Successful entries persist their intermediate snapshot as replay progress; failed entries restore only when the worktree still matches the queued target and retain their queue entry. Recovery recognizes a commit that landed before the queue update using its parent, subject, and file snapshots. The state mutex serializes holder and queue read-modify-write operations, and a mutex directory left without a PID is reclaimed after its initialization grace period.

Direct task checks capture HEAD before running the plan and compare it with HEAD after the plan using the commit-level drift inspector. A source-changing commit adds a required failed `worktree-drift` result, so the check exits nonzero and does not record reusable passing evidence. The inspector walks every commit reachable in `base..HEAD`, including side-branch commits, and compares merge commits with the first parent. That reports a source commit even if later reverted while avoiding false positives for changes already present at check start but absent from a merge's second parent. If ancestry or path inspection fails, the comparison fails closed. Messages include commit subjects and source paths.

An engineer already running can still write source files directly; RepoOS cannot fence arbitrary filesystem writes. RepoOS blocks a new managed engineer start under the lock and refuses its own source commits. Committed source edits during a check are caught by post-check drift and invalidate the result. This accepted boundary is documented in `docs/check-run-history.md`, `docs/agent-workflow-rules.md`, and `user-docs/check.md`.

## Approaches tried

For replay recovery, a simple progress cursor was insufficient because a process can crash after Git creates a commit but before the queue state advances. The on-disk pending journal lets recovery verify whether that exact commit landed and advance once. Focused tests first exposed that the synchronous replay path was mistakenly using async `runGit`; replacing those reads with `gitCapture` made replay proceed. Review 9's failure-path tests then found that a failed first entry had persisted the initial final snapshot as progress. I changed the journal write to preserve only previously committed progress, and let the pending record carry the temporary before-state.

For source protection, I kept the documented limitation instead of adding another filesystem guard: active engineers can bypass application-level write wrappers. The direct task check now validates commit-level drift before releasing its lock, and a production `cmdCheck` test commits a source edit inside its check step to prove the CLI fails with the subject and path.

## Challenges and blockers

The previous handoff reported a test failure on `mini` without naming the failing case. I reran the full required scoped check after these changes. The remote run hung on `thinkpad`; RepoOS killed that validation container and retried on `bee`, where the build and scoped tests passed, along with UI smoke and rendered contrast. Local formatting, lint, build, guards, smoke, and the user docs build also passed. Focused regression tests for all three flush paths and direct source drift passed. The mini failure did not reproduce on this run.

## Key learnings

The queue's durable state must represent both the intended snapshots and only the entries already committed. A failed replay also needs to preserve the lock fence, or subsequent commits can pass while an older queue is stranded. A mutex must cover the full read-modify-write sequence and recover the creation-before-PID crash window. Git inspection needs to enumerate all commits after the starting HEAD but compare each merge's own delta to its first parent. Direct filesystem-write protection has a firm boundary: managed starts and RepoOS writes can be guarded; already-running process writes are handled by after-the-fact drift detection.
